manifest.title: Order-invariant cluster first-order logic is included in first-order logic on bounded-degree graphs

inputs.abstract:
Order-invariant cluster first-order logic is included in first-order logic on bounded-degree graphs. A cluster first-order sentence is order-invariant if, on every finite graph over the given vocabulary, any two linear orders on its vertices give the sentence the same truth value. For every such sentence and every degree bound $d$, there is a first-order sentence over adjacency and the original unary predicates that agrees with it on all finite graphs of maximum degree at most $d$.

For each context depth $k$, we construct an order on a graph $A$ and transfer it to a graph $B$ that agrees with $A$ on first-order sentences up to a sufficiently large quantifier rank. On $A$, vertices of rare neighbourhood types initially form singleton blocks. We group the other vertices by their unary predicates and an auxiliary colour. At stage $i$ we choose the first and last vertices of each block, set apart the vertices close to those endpoints or to previously exceptional vertices, and split the remainder of each block by outer $i$-context. Any order extending the final sequence of blocks realises its set of context labels.

At depth $k$, put $r=k(k+1)/2$. Vertices are rare when their uncoloured radius-$r$ type occurs fewer than $t$ times. A finite threshold argument lets us choose $t$ large enough, relative to the number of rare vertices, to prescribe colours near the exceptional vertices and still realise every injective colouring of each frequent type elsewhere. The threshold and an upper bound on the number of exceptional vertices are determined from counts truncated at a uniform cap. We choose the first-order similarity rank to cover the count assertions and a sentence naming the full radius-$3r$ neighbourhood of the final exceptional set and identifying all rare vertices. We copy the auxiliary colours on its inner part and extend them to $B$. The images of the chosen endpoints determine the boundaries of the corresponding blocks. Their order and labels determine the sets of lower contexts between consecutive ball vertices and in the two outer intervals. The resulting orders realise the same outer $k$-contexts, so they agree on cluster sentences of quantifier rank at most $k+1$. Order invariance and first-order definability of the finitely many bounded-rank equivalence classes give the inclusion.

concepts.title: Order-invariant cluster first-order logic is included in first-order logic on bounded-degree graphs
concepts.description:
Fix a finite vocabulary consisting of adjacency and $c$ unary predicates.
A closed cluster first-order sentence $f$ over this vocabulary with an
additional linear order is order-invariant if, for every finite simple graph
$G$ over the vocabulary and every two linear orders on its vertices, $f$ has
the same truth value in the two ordered graphs. For every such $f$, every
natural number $d$, and every class $C$ of finite graphs of maximum degree
at most $d$, there exists a closed first-order sentence over adjacency and
the unary predicates that agrees with $f$ on every graph in $C$ under every
linear order on its vertices.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax266678.Definability

/-!
---
title: Order-invariant cluster first-order logic is included in first-order logic on bounded-degree graphs
type: theorem
---
Fix a finite vocabulary consisting of adjacency and $c$ unary predicates.
A closed cluster first-order sentence $f$ over this vocabulary with an
additional linear order is order-invariant if, for every finite simple graph
$G$ over the vocabulary and every two linear orders on its vertices, $f$ has
the same truth value in the two ordered graphs. For every such $f$, every
natural number $d$, and every class $C$ of finite graphs of maximum degree
at most $d$, there exists a closed first-order sentence over adjacency and
the unary predicates that agrees with $f$ on every graph in $C$ under every
linear order on its vertices.
-/
namespace Lax266678.Collapse
open Lax977378.Logic

axiom orderInvariantCFO_in_FO {c d : Nat} (C : Graph c → Prop)
    (bounded : ∀ G, C G → G.Bounded d) (f : Formula c) (legal : Legal [] f)
    (inv : ∀ G : Graph c, ∀ a b, Holds G a f ↔ Holds G b f) :
    ∃ φ : Formula c, Plain [] φ ∧ ∀ G, C G → ∀ a, Holds G a f ↔ Unordered G φ

end Lax266678.Collapse

statements.signature:
orderInvariantCFO_in_FO : ∀ {c d : Nat} (C : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c → Prop),
  (∀ (G : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c), C G → G.Bounded d) →
    ∀ (f : Lax977378.Logic.Formula c),
      Lax977378.Logic.Legal List.nil f →
        (∀ (G : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c) (a b : LinearOrder (Fin G.size)),
            Iff (Lax977378.Logic.Holds G a f) (Lax977378.Logic.Holds G b f)) →
          Exists fun φ =>
            And (Lax977378.Logic.Plain List.nil φ)
              (∀ (G : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c),
                C G →
                  ∀ (a : LinearOrder (Fin G.size)), Iff (Lax977378.Logic.Holds G a f) (Lax977378.Logic.Unordered G φ))

concepts.title: First-order definability from agreement at bounded rank
concepts.description:
Fix a finite graph vocabulary with $c$ unary predicates, a class $C$ of finite
graphs, a property $P$ of finite graphs and a natural number $q$. Suppose
that whenever two members of $C$ agree on all order-free first-order
sentences of quantifier rank at most $q$, either both have $P$ or neither
does. Then a single order-free first-order sentence defines $P$ on $C$.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax266678.Transfer

/-!
---
title: First-order definability from agreement at bounded rank
type: lemma
---
Fix a finite graph vocabulary with $c$ unary predicates, a class $C$ of finite
graphs, a property $P$ of finite graphs and a natural number $q$. Suppose
that whenever two members of $C$ agree on all order-free first-order
sentences of quantifier rank at most $q$, either both have $P$ or neither
does. Then a single order-free first-order sentence defines $P$ on $C$.
-/
namespace Lax266678.Definability
open Lax977378.Logic Lax266678.Transfer

axiom definable {c : Nat} (C P : Graph c → Prop) (q : Nat)
    (stable : ∀ A B, C A → C B → equivalentAt q A B → (P A ↔ P B)) :
    ∃ f : Formula c, Plain [] f ∧ ∀ A, C A → (P A ↔ Unordered A f)

end Lax266678.Definability

statements.signature:
definable : ∀ {c : Nat} (C P : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c → Prop) (q : Nat),
  (∀ (A B : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c), C A → C B → Lax266678.Transfer.equivalentAt q A B → Iff (P A) (P B)) →
    Exists fun f =>
      And (Lax977378.Logic.Plain List.nil f)
        (∀ (A : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c), C A → Iff (P A) (Lax977378.Logic.Unordered A f))

concepts.title: Transferring a refinement order between first-order equivalent graphs
concepts.description:
Fix $c$ unary predicates, a maximum degree $d$ and a context depth $k$.
There is a rank $q$ such that every finite simple graph $A$ of degree at most
$d$ admits a linear order $a$ with the following property. For every finite
simple graph $B$ in the same vocabulary of degree at most $d$ which agrees
with $A$ on every order-free first-order sentence of quantifier rank at most
$q$, there is a linear order $b$ on $B$ such that $(A,a)$ and $(B,b)$ realise
the same outer $k$-contexts. The source order is chosen before $B$.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax977378.OuterContexts

/-!
---
title: Transferring a refinement order between first-order equivalent graphs
type: theorem
---
Fix $c$ unary predicates, a maximum degree $d$ and a context depth $k$.
There is a rank $q$ such that every finite simple graph $A$ of degree at most
$d$ admits a linear order $a$ with the following property. For every finite
simple graph $B$ in the same vocabulary of degree at most $d$ which agrees
with $A$ on every order-free first-order sentence of quantifier rank at most
$q$, there is a linear order $b$ on $B$ such that $(A,a)$ and $(B,b)$ realise
the same outer $k$-contexts. The source order is chosen before $B$.
-/
namespace Lax266678.Transfer
open Lax977378.Logic Lax977378.OuterContexts

def equivalentAt {c : Nat} (q : Nat) (A B : Graph c) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : Formula c, Plain [] f → rank f ≤ q → (Unordered A f ↔ Unordered B f)

axiom transferOrder (c d k : Nat) : ∃ q : Nat, ∀ A : Graph c, A.Bounded d →
  ∃ a : LinearOrder (Fin A.size), ∀ B : Graph c, B.Bounded d → equivalentAt q A B →
    ∃ b : LinearOrder (Fin B.size), spectrumAgrees A B a b k

end Lax266678.Transfer

statements.signature:
transferOrder : ∀ (c d k : Nat),
  Exists fun q =>
    ∀ (A : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c),
      A.Bounded d →
        Exists fun a =>
          ∀ (B : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c),
            B.Bounded d →
              Lax266678.Transfer.equivalentAt q A B → Exists fun b => Lax977378.OuterContexts.spectrumAgrees A B a b k

concepts.title: Quantifier rank of a sentence describing counts and a marked neighbourhood
concepts.description:
Fix a finite graph vocabulary, a radius $r$ for pointed types, a window
radius $R$, a finite graph $W$ with two distinguished subsets of vertices,
a count cap $t$, a list of pointed types with prescribed counts up to $t$,
and a list of frequent types. Suppose all listed pointed patterns have at
most $b$ vertices, the prescribed counts are at most $t$, and $|W|\le U$.
There is an order-free first-order sentence of rank at most
$\max(b+r+t+4,U+\max(R,b+r)+5)$ with the following meaning.
Each specified count below $t$ is exact, and a count equal to $t$ is a
lower bound. There is an induced copy of $W$ whose vertex set is the full
radius-$R$ neighbourhood of the first distinguished subset. The image of
the second distinguished subset consists exactly of the vertices whose
radius-$r$ type is absent from the list of frequent types.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax977378.RecordTests

/-!
---
title: Quantifier rank of a sentence describing counts and a marked neighbourhood
type: lemma
---
Fix a finite graph vocabulary, a radius $r$ for pointed types, a window
radius $R$, a finite graph $W$ with two distinguished subsets of vertices,
a count cap $t$, a list of pointed types with prescribed counts up to $t$,
and a list of frequent types. Suppose all listed pointed patterns have at
most $b$ vertices, the prescribed counts are at most $t$, and $|W|\le U$.
There is an order-free first-order sentence of rank at most
$\max(b+r+t+4,U+\max(R,b+r)+5)$ with the following meaning.
Each specified count below $t$ is exact, and a count equal to $t$ is a
lower bound. There is an induced copy of $W$ whose vertex set is the full
radius-$R$ neighbourhood of the first distinguished subset. The image of
the second distinguished subset consists exactly of the vertices whose
radius-$r$ type is absent from the list of frequent types.
-/
namespace Lax266678.WindowRank
open Lax977378.Logic Lax977378.RecordTests

def bound (b r cap U R : Nat) : Nat := max (b+r+cap+4) (U+max R (b+r)+5)

axiom windowSentence {c : Nat} (D : TestData c) (b U : Nat)
    (counts : ∀ e ∈ D.counts, e.1.pattern.size ≤ b ∧ e.2 ≤ D.cap)
    (freq : ∀ e ∈ D.frequent, e.pattern.size ≤ b) (size : D.windowGraph.size ≤ U) :
    ∃ f : Formula c, Plain [] f ∧ rank f ≤ bound b D.radius D.cap U D.windowRadius ∧
      ∀ G, Unordered G f ↔ Passes D G

end Lax266678.WindowRank

statements.signature:
windowSentence : ∀ {c : Nat} (D : Lax977378.RecordTests.TestData c) (b U : Nat),
  (∀ (e : Prod (Lax977378.RecordTests.Pointed c) Nat),
      List.instMembership.mem D.counts e → And (instLENat.le e.fst.pattern.size b) (instLENat.le e.snd D.cap)) →
    (∀ (e : Lax977378.RecordTests.Pointed c), List.instMembership.mem D.frequent e → instLENat.le e.pattern.size b) →
      instLENat.le D.windowGraph.size U →
        Exists fun f =>
          And (Lax977378.Logic.Plain List.nil f)
            (And (instLENat.le (Lax977378.Logic.rank f) (Lax266678.WindowRank.bound b D.radius D.cap U D.windowRadius))
              (∀ (G : Lax977378.Logic.Graph c), Iff (Lax977378.Logic.Unordered G f) (Lax977378.RecordTests.Passes D G)))

proofs.description:
A tuple profile consists of its atomic diagram and, recursively, the finite
set of profiles obtained by adjoining one vertex. Equal depth-q profiles
give the same truth values to all order-free formulas of rank at most q,
by induction on formulas. Take one graph per realised empty-tuple profile
in the class. Separate each positive representative from each negative
representative by a rank-bounded sentence and form the finite Boolean combination.

Choose context depth one less than the quantifier rank, using depth zero for
rank zero. Transfer the source order, compare the ordered graphs at that
depth, and use order invariance on each graph to obtain a property constant
on bounded-rank first-order classes.

Bound the number of rare vertices and the size of the exceptional neighbourhood
before choosing either graph. The bound on the number of window vertices and the maximum size of a
pointed neighbourhood pattern give an explicit rank budget for the count and
induced-neighbourhood sentence. Choose the source colouring, the refinement order and its endpoints.
Rank equivalence transfers the actual source neighbourhood sentence to the target.
Copy the inner colouring, realise the frequent coloured types away from the
exceptional vertices, and transfer the source order along the resulting window.

Build a sentence by existentially naming the window vertices, specifying their
induced diagram, and checking exact neighbourhood coverage and rarity. Compile
bounded distance, rooted types and count inequalities with a rank budget that
is preserved by finite Boolean combinations.
